column2: You go on the path of making things known, and are skilled in secrets; yet you are surely not honoured by those who know it; so you are pale and lean.
Your virtues do not shine among the wicked who are obstinate, to whom you speak with all doubt cast off; so you are pale and lean.
Lacking wealth, wisdom and learning, and having only energy, you aspire to something great; so you are pale and lean.
I think you are set on austerity and long for the forest, but your kinsmen do not accept it; so you are pale and lean.
Surely your excellent word does not shine among men of means, spoken at the wrong time; so you are pale and lean.
You cannot win over a fool fixed in his old ideas, angry and dear to your heart; so you are pale and lean.
Surely, after attaching you to some desired task, someone asks too much of you; so you are pale and lean.
Surely a friend, honouring you for your own virtues, knows "he is for my purpose"; so you are pale and lean.
Surely you do not wish out of shame to speak the intent within you, from slackness in attaining it; so you are pale and lean.
Surely you wish to win over, by your own virtues, men in the world of all minds and tastes; so you are pale and lean.
Unlearned, timid and of little means, you surely seek fame born of knowledge, valour and giving; so you are pale and lean.
Some fruit long desired has not been yours; others have done it and carried it off; so you are pale and lean.
Surely, seeing no fault of your own in yourself, you are blamed without cause; so you are pale and lean.
Grief born from the loss of what cannot be recovered from careful friends, lacking the virtues of wealth; so you are pale and lean.
Seeing householders who are good and forest-dwellers who are not, and the liberated who are attached to dwellings; so you are pale and lean.
Your word, rightful and spoken in the right time and place, does not take hold; so you are pale and lean.
You live, a wise man wishing to live, on wealth given by the unskilled; so you are pale and lean.
Seeing the wicked thrive and the good decline, you surely seek a fit remedy; so you are pale and lean.
Surely you wish to please mutually opposed friends without opposing any of them; so you are pale and lean.
I think you brood over learned men engaged in wrong deeds, and wise men who have not conquered their senses; so you are pale and lean."
Thus honoured, the rakshasa honoured the brahmin in return, made him his friend, and, rewarding him with wealth, released him.
I wish to hear from you, scourge of foes, what is joined with dharma and wealth, and brings happiness in the future, a marvel to the world.
This time has come, when kinsmen and relatives are hard to find, and we have no teacher but you, best of the Bharatas.
If I, with my brothers, deserve your favour, blameless one, you should answer the question I ask you, O king.
This glorious Narayana, honoured by all kings, serves you with great respect and humility.
In his presence and before all the kings, you should speak to me for my brothers' pleasure, out of affection.
[Vaishampayana] Hearing his words, Bhishma, son of Bhagirathi, moved with affection and agitation, said these words.
Come, I shall tell you a most delightful tale: this power of Vishnu, O king, I heard long ago.
Hear from me too the power of him who bears the bull on his banner, and the doubt of Rudrani, and of the couple.
The son of Devaki, pleased, arranged for them the guest-honour proper to the family, fit for gods.
On green, golden and new seats of kusha, the great sages sat down, pleased.
Then they told sweet tales full of dharma, of royal sages and of the gods, of those ascetics who dwell there.
Then, from the mouth of Krishna, of marvellous deeds, a Narayana fire, a radiance risen from the fuel of vows and austerity, came out.
That fire burned the mountain, with its trees, creepers and shrubs, its flocks of birds and deer, its beasts of prey and reptiles.
With animals of many forms crying out, senseless, the peak of that mountain was churned and bright to see.
That fire of great flames, having burned everything entire, came to Vishnu and touched his feet like a pupil.
Then Vishnu, scourge of foes, seeing the forest burned, restored it with his gentle glances to its natural state.
So the mountain again had flowering creepers and trees, resounded with flocks of birds, and had beasts of prey and reptiles.
Seeing that marvellous, inconceivable thing, the company of sages was amazed, their hair bristling and their eyes tearful.
Then Narayana, best of speakers, seeing those sages amazed, asked them humbly, sweetly and kindly:

What amazement has come to this company of sages, who have always given up attachment, without possessiveness and learned in the texts?
mahabharata:13:126.25	Blameless ascetics, the sages should tell me all this doubt as it truly is, with settled purpose.
[The sages] "You release the worlds and you withdraw them again. You are the cold, you the heat, you alone rain down.
Of the beings on earth, moving and unmoving, you are father and mother, lord and origin.
Explain to us this marvel, Madhusudana; you alone are fit to tell, auspicious one, the going forth of the fire.
Then, scourge of foes, we too, free of fear, will tell what we have heard and seen, Hari."
[Vasudeva] "This was that Vaishnava radiance that came from my mouth, the black-pathed one, bright as the end of the yuga, by which this mountain was churned.
You sages, who have conquered anger and your senses, fell into distress; you, divine ascetics, were pained.
From me, pleased with the practice of vows and with the service of ascetics' vows, the fire arose; you should not be pained.
I came to this fair mountain to keep a vow, and came to create by austerity a son equal to myself in valour.
Then that which is my self in the body went out as fire, and went to see the boon-giver, the grandfather of all worlds.
By him I was instructed, O best of sages, 'With half your radiance, a son will be yours, bearing the bull banner.'
That fire, having come to my feet, served me like a pupil and returned, calmed, to its natural state.
This is the secret of the wise Padmanabha, told to you by me with love; do not fear, ascetics.
You have unobstructed passage everywhere, far-sighted, kindled by the vows of ascetics, adorned with knowledge and wisdom.
Whatever marvel you have heard or seen, in heaven or on earth, tell it to me."

I long for the honey of your speech, like nectar, told here by you who dwell in the ascetic forest.
mahabharata:13:126.41	Even if I see something unseen, divine, wondrous to behold, in heaven or on earth, O you of pure sight,
mahabharata:13:126.42	that is my supreme nature, nowhere obstructed, and the power within me does not seem a marvel to me.
mahabharata:13:126.43	A matter told that is credible, once it has gone into good men's ears, endures long on earth like writing set on stone.
mahabharata:13:126.44	What has come from the mouths of good men, I shall tell in their company, day after day, a lamp to men's understanding.
Then all the company of sages, humble before Krishna, looked at Janardana with eyes like lotus petals.
Some blessed him and others honoured him, praising Madhusudana in words filled with Rik verses.
Then all the company of sages appointed Narada, of divine sight, skilled in speech, to speak.

The marvel and the inconceivable thing, lord, that the company of sages, intent on pilgrimage, experienced on the Himalaya,
mahabharata:13:126.49	do you, urged by all, tell Hrishikesha entire, as seen, for the good of the host of sages.
Thus addressed by the sages, the blessed sage Narada, the divine seer, told a fair tale of former events.
The righteous lord of the gods, bearing the bull banner, practised austerity on the holy Himalaya, frequented by siddhas and charanas.
It was charming, full of many herbs, thick with many flowers, crowded with troops of apsarases and frequented by hosts of spirits.
There the god, joyful, surrounded by hundreds of hosts of spirits of many forms, deformed, divine and wondrous to see,
like lions, tigers and elephants, of every kind, with faces of jackals and leopards, bears and bulls,
with faces of owls, terrible ones, with faces of hawks, like deer of many colours, of every kind, with kinnaras, gods, gandharvas, yakshas and hosts of spirits;
strewn with divine flowers, adorned with divine garlands, joined with divine sandal, perfumed with divine incense, that hall of the bull-bannered god resounded with divine instruments,
sounding with drums and tabors, with conches and kettledrums, with hosts of spirits dancing all around, and with peacocks.
With apsarases dancing, served by troops of divine women, delightful to the eye, indescribable, divine, wondrous to behold.
Resounding with brahmins intent on study, with the sound of the Veda, and with the songs of bees, the mountain was like Madhava's.
Seeing that terrible form, like a great festival, great joy arose in the company of sages, Janardana.
The sages of great fortune, the siddhas with upward-turned seed, the Maruts, Vasus, Sadhyas and the eternal Vishvedevas,
yakshas, nagas, pishachas, the guardians of the world, the fires, and all the beings of the lower orders were assembled there.
The seasons scattered all manner of flowers, wondrously, and the blazing herbs lit up that forest.
Birds, joyful, danced and sang on the charming ridges of the mountain, calling pleasantly to people.
There the god, great-minded, sat on the mountainside adorned with divine minerals, shining as if on a couch.
Wearing a tiger-skin garment and a lion-skin covering, with a serpent for sacred thread, and red armlets for ornaments,
green-bearded, matted-haired, terrible, the terror of the gods' enemies, yet fearless to all beings and to devotees, the bull-bannered god.
Seeing him, all the sages bowed their heads to the earth, freed from all sins, forgiven, their stains gone.
The abode of that lord of beings shone, of terrible form, harder to approach and thronged with great serpents.
In an instant everything became marvellous, Madhusudana; that hall of the bull-bannered god shone, taking on a terrible form.
The mountain's daughter approached him, surrounded by troops of female spirits, wearing garments like Hara's, keeping the same vows.
Bearing a golden pitcher with water from all the tirthas, auspicious, followed on all sides by holy mountain streams,
raining down a shower of flowers and many perfumes, she served the Himalaya's side and came to Hara's side.
Then, smiling, the fair-looking goddess, playfully, suddenly covered Hara's fair eyes with her two hands.
With the eyes covered, darkness fell, senseless; that hall suddenly became without oblation and without vashat.
All the people, dismayed and seized with fear and terror, were as if the sun were lost when the lord of beings closed his eyes.
Then in an instant the world became free of darkness, and a great blazing flame came out of his forehead.
A third eye appeared on him, like the sun, blazing like the end of the yuga, by which that mountain was churned.
Then the mountain's daughter, seeing him whose eyes were like blazing fire, bowed her head to Hara, her eyes wide.
As that forest burned, with its sala, sarala and other trees, the lovely sandalwood grove, bright with divine herbs,
herds of deer, fled and fearful, came to Hara's side; finding no refuge, that hall shone, crowded.
Then a flame touching the sky, bright as lightning and the light of the worlds, like the twelve Adityas, was like another fire of the end of the yuga.
In that instant the Himalaya, the mountain, was burnt, its peaks of minerals ablaze, and its forest and herbs miserably burned.
Seeing that mountain churned, the mountain king's daughter then took refuge in the blessed one and stood with folded hands.
Then Sharva, seeing Uma softened by womanly tenderness, unwilling to see her father's distress, looked on the mountain with love.
Then all became again as before, lovely to see, with birds delighted and trees of the forest in full flower.
Seeing the mountain restored, the goddess was pleased, and the blameless one spoke to Maheshvara, her husband, lord of all beings.

Blessed one, lord of all beings, trident in hand, of great vows, a great doubt has arisen in me; you should explain it to me.
mahabharata:13:127.41	Why has a third eye risen on your forehead? Why was the mountain burned, with its flocks of birds and forests?
mahabharata:13:127.42	And why, god, was it restored in an instant to its natural state, covered again with trees, Maheshvara?
[Maheshvara] "Goddess, blameless one, when you closed my eyes in play, the world lost its light in an instant.
When the sun was lost and the world became dark, O mountain's daughter, I made the third eye blaze to protect creatures.
From that eye came the great fire by which this mountain was churned; and for your pleasure, goddess, I restored it in an instant."
[Uma] "Blessed one, by what is your face pleasing to see like the moon, and so lovely in the east, and likewise the north and the west?
By what is your south face terrible, by what are your matted locks tawny above, by what is your neck made blue like a peacock's tail?
Why does this Pinaka always stay in your hand, and why are you always matted-haired and celibate?
Tell me all this doubt, lord of beings, blameless one; I am your dharma-following wife and devoted, bull-bannered one."
Thus addressed by the mountain's daughter, the blessed bearer of Pinaka was pleased with her conduct and her understanding.
Then the god said to her: "Fair one, hear by what reasons I have these forms, lovely-faced one."

Goddess, you approached me, incomparable in beauty on earth, fair-faced, circling me and tempting me, auspicious one.
mahabharata:13:128.3	Wherever that fair-toothed one ran to me, there, goddess, a lovely face of mine appeared.
mahabharata:13:128.4	Wishing to see her, I by yoga became four-formed, and became four-faced, showing my yoga.
mahabharata:13:128.5	With the east face I rule as Indra; with the north I delight with you, blameless one.
mahabharata:13:128.6	My west face is gentle and brings happiness to all beings; the south is terrible and fierce and withdraws creatures.
mahabharata:13:128.7	I am matted-haired and celibate, desiring the good of the worlds; for accomplishing the gods' work, the Pinaka is in my hand.
mahabharata:13:128.8	Long ago Indra, desiring glory, hurled his thunderbolt at me; it burned my throat and went, and so I have the name Shrikantha (blue throat).
[Uma] "Though you have many splendid vehicles, god, how did the bull become your vehicle?"
In a place frightful with hair and bones, crowded with skull-pots, with vultures and jackals, crowded with hundreds of funeral pyres,
unclean, thick with flesh, a mire of fat and blood, heaped with scattered flesh, resounding with the howls of jackals,
[Maheshvara] "I seek what is pure and wander over the whole earth at night, and nothing here is purer than the cremation ground.
So of all dwellings my mind delights in the cremation ground, covered with banyan branches, adorned with discarded garlands.
There the hosts of spirits delight me, fair-faced one, and I cannot live, goddess, without the hosts of spirits.
This dwelling is pure to me and is held to be heavenly; it is holy and supreme, resorted to by those who desire purity."
[Uma] "Blessed one, lord of all beings, best of those who uphold all dharma, Pinaka-bearer, boon-giver, this is a great doubt for me.
All this company of sages, lord, says "austerity, austerity"; the austerity-seeker wanders in the world in many forms.
For the pleasure of this host of sages and me, you should tell me this doubt here, scourge of foes.
What is the mark of dharma said to be, and how can men practise it who have not found dharma? Knower of dharma, tell me, lord."
[Narada] Then the whole company of sages honoured the goddess with words filled with Rik verses and with praises, O best of those who know meaning.
[Maheshvara] "Non-harm, truthful speech, compassion for all beings, calm, giving as one is able: the householder's dharma is supreme.
Not setting the mind on another's wife, protection of deposits and of women, abstaining from taking what is not given, giving up honey and meat.
This is the fivefold dharma, with many branches and rising in happiness; embodied beings devoted to dharma should accumulate it.
[Uma] Blessed one, asked about a doubt, explain to me the dharma of the four classes that brings virtue in each class.
What is the dharma of a brahmin, what that of a kshatriya, what is the mark of dharma in a vaishya, and what in a shudra?
[Maheshvara] Your doubt is rightly raised, fortunate one. Brahmins, the twice-born, are always the great gods of the earth in the world.
Fasting is always the dharma of a brahmin, without doubt; for he is born for dharma and is fit to become one with Brahman.
For him, goddess, the rites of dharma, the practice of vows, and also the initiation properly belong to the twice-born.
The practice of study, for the worship of teachers and gods, is the source of dharma and should be practised by embodied beings devoted to dharma.
[Uma] Blessed one, I have a doubt on this; explain it to me. Tell skilfully the dharma of the four classes.
[Maheshvara] Hearing secrets, keeping the Vedic vows, practising vows as supreme dharma, and pleasing the teacher's feet are dharma.
Begging is supreme dharma, constant fasting is dharma, constant study is dharma, and so is the student's stage of life.
Permitted by the teacher, the twice-born should return home, and then take a wife suitable, by rule.
Avoiding a shudra's food is dharma, as is following the path of the good; constant fasting and celibacy are dharma.
The householder who keeps the fire, studies, offers oblations, controls his senses, eats what is left, eats moderately, is truthful and pure,
devotion to guests is dharma, keeping the three fires is dharma; he should duly perform the Ishtis and animal rites.
Sacrifice is supreme dharma, and so is non-harm toward embodied beings; eating no unprecedented food is dharma, and eating what is left.
Eating after the household has eaten is called dharma, for a brahmin householder, especially a learned one.
Similarity of character in the couple is the dharma of householders; and the daily offering of flowers and food to the household gods.
Daily smearing and daily fasting are dharma, and a house well swept and plastered, with smoke rising from ghee.
This is the householder's dharma among the twice-born, which upholds the world, and it goes on always among the good twice-born.
As for the dharma you asked about, goddess, concerning the kshatriya, I shall tell you that; hear it from me attentively.
The kshatriya's dharma is held to be above all protecting subjects; a king who enjoys the fruit prescribed is joined with dharma.
The king who protects subjects with dharma has worlds won by dharma, accumulated by protecting subjects.
There the king's supreme dharma is self-control and study, tending the fire, giving and learning.
Supporting dependants is dharma, and not leaving a task done in vain.
Standing in right punishment is dharma, Vedic sacrifices are dharma, standing in lawful dealing is dharma, and delight in truthful speech.
A king who extends a hand to the distressed is honoured after death and here. One who fights for cows and brahmins and dies in battle wins the worlds won by the Ashvamedha, in the abode of heaven.
For a vaishya the dharma is always herding and farming, tending the fire, giving and learning.
Trade, standing on the good path, hospitality, calm and self-control, welcoming brahmins, and giving are the eternal dharma of a vaishya.
He should never sell sesame, perfumes or juices; a vaishya who keeps the merchant's road stays on the good path.
Hospitality to all, as one is able and as is fitting, is the dharma of the three; the supreme dharma of a shudra is always service to the twice-born.
A shudra of sharpened austerity, true to his word and master of his senses, serving a guest who has come, stores up great austerity.
Giving up harm, of good conduct, honouring gods and the twice-born, a wise shudra may be joined with the desired fruits of dharma.
All this has been told to you, auspicious one, of the four classes, each in its own way; what else do you wish to hear?
[Maheshvara] Brahmins were created by the Creator, desiring excellence, from the essence of the world, to carry all the worlds across; gods of the earth among mortals.
I shall tell you their dharma and the rise of the fruit of their deeds; the dharma that is in brahmins is held to be supreme dharma.
These three were created by the Self-existent for the world's dharma and wealth; they were always created in the making of the earth; hear them too from me.
Supreme dharma is that declared in the Veda; another is that found in the smriti texts; another, called supreme, is that practised by the good: these three dharmas are eternal.
A learned brahmin of the three Vedas, who does not live by teaching, who does three acts and has gone through three stages, is held to be a friend, a twice-born.
The Lord of the world declared these six acts for the livelihood of brahmins; hear them attentively.
Sacrificing, officiating, giving and receiving, teaching and learning: the twice-born with six acts shares in dharma.
Constant study is dharma, sacrifice is eternal dharma, and giving is praised for him, as one is able and by rule.
Pure in self by the five sacrifices, truthful, free of envy, a giver, honouring brahmins, with a well-swept house,
free of pride, straightforward, gentle in speech, generous, delighting in guests and visitors, eating what remains of his food:
he who gives foot-water, offering, seat, bed, lamp and shelter is righteous.
Rising in the morning, rinsing his mouth, inviting a guest to a meal, honouring and following him: that is his eternal dharma.
Hospitality to all, to the extent of one's ability, day and night, is the dharma told for the shudra: serving the three classes.
The dharma marked by action is ordained for householders. I shall tell it: it is auspicious and good for all beings.
One should give repeatedly as able, sacrifice repeatedly, and perform nourishing rites, if desiring well-being.
Wealth should be gathered by dharma; wealth gained by dharma should be in three parts, and a man should earnestly keep dharma supreme.
One part should be used for dharma and wealth by one who desires prosperity, one part for desire and wealth, and one part he should increase.
The other dharma, marked by withdrawal, is held to be liberation. I shall tell its practice; hear it from me truly, goddess.
Compassion for all beings is dharma, and not living in one village; freedom from the snare of hope is praised for seekers of liberation.
No attachment to a water-pot, to water, to clothing, to a seat, to a triple staff, to a bed, to fire, or to a shelter.
One whose mind is on the Self, whose thought is on that, who is devoted to it, always attentive to yoga and to reflection,
who always sleeps at the foot of a tree, dwells in empty houses, sleeps on river banks and delights in riverside,
freed from all attachments and bonds of affection, the twice-born who wanders fixing his mind only on the Self in the Self.
Becoming like a post, without food, by the action seen for liberation, one who wanders disciplined has the eternal dharma.
Not long attached to one place, not confined to one village, he wanders disciplined and free, not sleeping on one riverbank.
This is the dharma of the knowers of liberation, the good path of the good, declared in the Veda; for one who follows this path, there is no further step.
Mendicants are of four kinds: the hut-dweller, the water-maker, the hamsa and the paramahamsa; each later one is higher.
Beyond this there is nothing higher, nothing lower, nothing across or ahead: painless, pleasureless, gentle, ageless, deathless, imperishable.
[Uma] You have told the householder's dharma and the dharma of liberation as practised by the good, the great path of the world of mortals leading to the best.
But I wish to hear the supreme dharma of the sages, knower of dharma; I always long for the dwellers in the ascetic forest.
Though so afflicted by Samvarta, the king still followed that sage with folded hands, trying to appease him.
Yuyutsu and Sanjaya: I shall do that straightaway, for all these are to be honoured by me, being well-wishers of this family.
He, lord of the world, who by valour slew Keshin and Kamsa and made lifeless the Chedi king proud of his strength, Partha.
Uttara with his brother Shankha, best of men, entered the Vishvedevas, those best of men.
